Let’s dive into Chapter Three: Establishing Baselines—The Importance of Context and Consistency.
You know, nonverbal cues can give you some incredible insights into what someone’s really thinking or feeling. But here’s the thing—those signals only truly make sense if you understand the context behind them. After all, people aren’t robots; our moods shift, our environments change, and the people we’re with can make a big difference in how we behave.
So, if you want to really understand what someone’s telling you—without words—you’ve got to start by establishing a baseline. Think of it as learning what’s “normal” for that person.
What exactly is a baseline? Well, it’s the usual way someone acts, speaks, and expresses themselves. It’s your personal reference point. Without this, even the sharpest observer can end up reading things wrong.
For example, maybe you work with two people. One always talks fast and waves their hands, while the other is naturally quiet and reserved. If the outgoing one suddenly goes silent, that’s worth noticing. But if the reserved person is just being their usual quiet self, there’s probably nothing unusual going on. So, how do you actually set a baseline?
First, spend time observing someone in a variety of situations—see how they act when they’re relaxed, or when they’re under stress, or even just chatting with friends versus talking to strangers.
Next, pay attention to patterns. Does their voice always stay at the same pitch? Do they usually smile when they greet someone? These little habits matter.
And don’t forget, sometimes a casual conversation can do wonders. If you ask subtle, friendly questions, you’ll get a sense of what they’re like when they’re at ease.
Now, let’s talk about context. The same person will act totally differently at a family dinner compared to a job interview. Culture, social expectations, even the time of day—these things all play a role. If you want to be a great people-reader, you’ve got to consider all these factors before you start interpreting what you see.
Once you’ve got a baseline, the magic happens. Deviations—those little changes in tone, posture, or energy—suddenly stand out. If your usually cheerful friend turns quiet during a conversation, there’s a good chance something’s up.
Here’s a practical example: Imagine you’re at the negotiation table. You’ve noticed the buyer is usually very calm and collected. But when the topic of price comes up, they start fidgeting and can’t quite meet your eye. That’s a clear shift from their baseline, and it might signal hesitation or discomfort. That’s your cue to pause, check in, or maybe tweak your approach.
Of course, there are some common traps to avoid. Don’t jump to conclusions just because you notice a single change in behavior. Look for patterns, or clusters of signals, before you decide what’s really going on.
Also, be careful not to project your own feelings onto someone else. Stay objective—focus on what you can actually see and hear, not what you imagine might be happening.
And remember, everyone’s different. What looks like anxiety in one person might be totally normal for another.
So, here’s the key takeaway: By grounding your observations in context and consistency, you’ll start to interpret signals with a whole new level of accuracy. This is how you turn surface-level observations into real, meaningful insight—and set yourself up for deeper understanding in every interaction.
